claims.text: Texas Health and Safety Code Section 183.005 is headed Artificial Intelligence in Electronic Health Record.
claims.quote: Sec. 183.005. ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE IN ELECTRONIC HEALTH RECORD.
claims.document: Texas Health and Safety Code Chapter 183, Electronic Health Records

claims.text: The section lets a health care practitioner use AI for diagnostic purposes if listed conditions are met. Those purposes include recommendations on a diagnosis or course of treatment based on a patient's medical record.
claims.quote: (a) A health care practitioner may use artificial intelligence for diagnostic purposes, including the use of artificial intelligence for recommendations on a diagnosis or course of treatment based on a patient's medical record, if:
claims.document: Texas Health and Safety Code Chapter 183, Electronic Health Records

claims.text: One condition is that the practitioner acts within the scope of the practitioner's license, certification or other authorization in Texas, whether or not AI is used.
claims.quote: (1) the practitioner is acting within the scope of the practitioner's license, certification, or other authorization to provide health care services in this state, regardless of the use of artificial intelligence
claims.document: Texas Health and Safety Code Chapter 183, Electronic Health Records

claims.text: Another is that the particular use of AI is not otherwise restricted or prohibited by state or federal law.
claims.quote: (2) the particular use of artificial intelligence is not otherwise restricted or prohibited by state or federal law
claims.document: Texas Health and Safety Code Chapter 183, Electronic Health Records

claims.text: The practitioner must also review all records created with AI in a manner consistent with medical records standards developed by the Texas Medical Board.
claims.quote: (3) the practitioner reviews all records created with artificial intelligence in a manner that is consistent with medical records standards developed by the Texas Medical Board.
claims.document: Texas Health and Safety Code Chapter 183, Electronic Health Records

claims.text: A practitioner who uses AI for diagnostic purposes as the section describes must disclose that use to the practitioner's patients.
claims.quote: (b) A health care practitioner who uses artificial intelligence for diagnostic purposes as described by Subsection (a) must disclose the practitioner's use of that technology to the practitioner's patients.
claims.document: Texas Health and Safety Code Chapter 183, Electronic Health Records

claims.text: The section was added by Senate Bill 1188 of the 89th Legislature in 2025.
claims.quote: Added by Acts 2025, 89th Leg., R.S., Ch. 1002 (S.B. 1188
claims.document: Texas Health and Safety Code Chapter 183, Electronic Health Records

claims.text: The section took effect September 1st, 2025.
claims.quote: Sec. 1, eff. September 1, 2025.
claims.document: Texas Health and Safety Code Chapter 183, Electronic Health Records

rejected.finding: Sec. 183.005 requires UTMB, or UTMB clinicians, to disclose OpenEvidence use to patients
rejected.reason: Subsection (b) binds a health care practitioner who uses AI for diagnostic purposes as Subsection (a) describes. It binds a practitioner, not an institution. No fetched source says OpenEvidence use at UTMB counts as diagnostic purposes. The release calls it clinical decision support and access to cited medical evidence. The record can state what the statute says (c18 to c25) and what UTMB says (c1 to c17). It can't link the two.

rejected.finding: UTMB published an accuracy, error rate or patient outcome figure for OpenEvidence
rejected.reason: The UTMB release has no such figure. The only quantity in it is more than half of UTMB clinicians (c9). Growth is described only as strong growth with no numbers. UTMB says it will continue evaluating utilization and clinician experience (c17) and reports no evaluation result.

rejected.finding: A count of UTMB clinicians using OpenEvidence or of queries submitted
rejected.reason: The release gives neither number, nor the size of the clinician base behind more than half.

rejected.finding: The Qualified Health contract (Regents consent item 65) pays for OpenEvidence
rejected.reason: Item 65 names only Qualified Health products. OpenEvidence does not appear in the item. Only item 65 and its neighbouring pages were read.

rejected.finding: The Board of Regents approved the Qualified Health third amendment
rejected.reason: The fetched document is the agenda book, which shows item 65 on the consent agenda for August 12th to 13th, 2026. No minutes or vote record was fetched.

rejected.finding: Any patient disclosure practice at UTMB for OpenEvidence or other AI
rejected.reason: The UTMB release says nothing about telling patients, notice, consent or disclosure. No other fetched source covers UTMB's practice.

rejected.finding: OpenEvidence went live at UTMB in March 2026
rejected.reason: The release says only went live at UTMB in March, with no year.

rejected.finding: OpenEvidence's About page statements stated as fact
rejected.reason: These are the vendor's statements about itself and are kept as primary_corporate claims attributed to OpenEvidence (c37 to c39).

rejected.finding: OpenEvidence's projection that more than 100 million Americans will be treated by a clinician using it this year
rejected.reason: A forward-looking vendor projection that could be confused with UTMB's more than 100 clinics (c12).

rejected.finding: The PubMed study's publication date and journal
rejected.reason: No contiguous verbatim string could be confirmed.

rejected.finding: Which named authors belong to MD Anderson and which to UTMB
rejected.reason: The affiliation element maps departments to initials only, so the record names institutions only (c41).
